hookLine: crusaders massacre the Jewish communities of the Rhineland

cards: On a Sabbath morning in a synagogue that follows the Ashkenazi custom, after the Torah reading, the congregation says a short memorial prayer. It begins with two Hebrew words, av harachamim, father of mercy.
It asks God to remember the holy communities who gave their lives, and it doesn't name them. It doesn't need to.
Tradition connects that prayer to the towns we met on the Rhine, Speyer, Worms and Mainz, and to the spring when armed bands on their way to a crusade came through them.
Today's lesson is named for that year: ten ninety-six.

teach.b: Our main witnesses are Hebrew chronicles written by Jews of the Rhineland, telling what happened to their own families. They read like lists and like laments at once.
Bands of crusaders, and townspeople who joined them, turned on the Jewish quarters as they marched.
In Speyer, the chronicles say, the bishop took the Jews under his protection, and fewer were lost there. In Worms, families who had sheltered in the bishop's palace were not safe there for long.
In Mainz, the community had paid for protection, and the protection failed.
Again and again the attackers offered the same choice: baptism or death. The chronicles tell of people baptized under that threat, and of others who refused, and they record both with sorrow.
Tomorrow we'll look at how Jewish tradition understood those who chose to die rather than give up their faith. Today is simply for memory.
The chronicles also name people who helped, a bishop who sheltered, a neighbor who hid someone; they are careful about who did what. The communities did not end.
Survivors returned, and some who had been forced into baptism came home to Judaism; the rulers allowed it. Synagogues were rebuilt. Students went on studying.
And the names were kept, written in memorial books and read aloud on certain Sabbaths, so that a family in a small town would not be forgotten.
That is the work of memory here: not drama, not anger used as a tool, but names, said out loud.

how: In Ashkenazi synagogues the memorial prayer Av HaRachamim is said after the Torah reading on Sabbaths, except on some festive ones, and some communities kept memorial books listing the names of those killed.

games.q: you survived the attacks, and the names of those killed are on everyone's lips. how does the community make sure they are remembered?
o: write the names in memorial books and read them aloud on certain Sabbaths.
leave the region and forget the towns.
games.why: communities kept memorial books and read the names aloud, and a Sabbath prayer, father of mercy, remembers the holy communities.

practice: If you have a candle and it's safe, light it now; if not, picture one, and watch the flame.
Bring to mind Speyer, Worms and Mainz, families at their tables, students at their books; you don't need to know their names, because the memorial books kept them.
If you pray, you can remember them in your own words, or with the words father of mercy.

wordCard.voice: Av harachamim. Father of mercy, the Sabbath memorial prayer that remembers, without naming, the Jewish communities of the Rhineland killed in 1096. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: father of mercy, the opening words of the Sabbath memorial prayer.

carryVoice: Your line: the rhineland. Its towns are still remembered in prayer today. See you tomorrow.
